summary: A guide that gives basic information so anyone on the network can start trying out network resource tools. It is FYI 23.

eli5.summary: A beginner's toolbox guide that shows what each tool on the Internet does and how to pick it up.

subtitle: A 1994 guide to network tools for exploring and sharing Internet resources.

tldr.problem: The rapid expansion of network resources makes it hard for users to discover and access information, files, discussion groups and people across the Internet.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes twelve major tools organized by function: Gopher and World-Wide Web for browsing networked information, WAIS for searching databases, ARCHIE for finding files, WHOIS/X.500/NETFIND for locating people and computers, TRICKLE/BITFTP for efficient file retrieval, LISTSERV/Netnews for discussion groups, plus six additional tools for specialized use.
tldr.outcome: By March 1994, most tools work via client-server architecture, accessible through local or remote clients, with internet access required for full functionality and email-only alternatives where available.

today: RFC 1580 is a historical document from 1994 describing network tools of that era. Most tools covered (Gopher, WAIS, ARCHIE, X.500) have faded from widespread use, supplanted by the Web. USENET (Netnews) and email-based tools remain in limited use. The document is valuable as a snapshot of pre-Web Internet information infrastructure.

sections.title: Overview of Network Tools
sections.content:
The RFC provides a practical guide to network resource tools for users who want to explore the rapidly expanding Internet. As academic and research networks grow, the number of available resources—texts, data, software and information—multiplies. The guide assumes basic familiarity with electronic mail, FTP (file transfer protocol) and Telnet (remote login).

The tools described use the client-server model. Special software on a server accepts requests and sends responses automatically. Users can run client software on their local computer or access a remote client via Telnet. Many servers also accept requests via email, allowing access even for those not on the Internet. The guide groups tools by their primary purpose: browsing information, searching databases, locating resources, finding people, retrieving files and participating in discussions.
sections.eli5: The Internet has so much information that you need tools to find what you want. This guide shows you twelve tools, each designed for a specific job.

sections.title: Browsing Tools: Gopher and World-Wide Web
sections.content:
Gopher, developed at the University of Minnesota, is a distributed document delivery service. It presents information as nested menus resembling a directory structure, with items that may reside on local or remote servers. From the user's perspective, all information appears seamless. Items can be text files, binary files, images, sounds, directory information or links to other services. Veronica is a search tool that indexes more than 500 Gopher menus, helping users find information without browsing menu-by-menu.

World-Wide Web (WWW), developed at CERN, is based on hypertext—linked documents where selected words or concepts point to related documents. The reader can follow links without knowing where the referenced document is located. Hypertext actually refers to hypermedia since links can point to images, video and sound. WWW provides access to many other tools described in the guide and can search indexes to find relevant documents.

Both tools use the client-server model. Public domain clients are available for Macintosh, MS-DOS, OS/2, VMS, NeXT, Unix and X-Windows. Remote access is available via Telnet, and email-based access exists for both tools.
sections.eli5: Gopher and the Web are like two different ways to browse the Internet. Gopher shows nested menus; the Web uses clickable links between documents. Both let you jump between computers seamlessly.

sections.title: Searching and Finding Tools
sections.content:
WAIS (Wide Area Information Server) is a distributed system for searching databases. Users do not need to learn different database query languages; WAIS accepts natural language queries and returns documents containing the query words. Databases cover topics from agriculture to social science, and may contain text, sound, pictures or video.

ARCHIE solves the problem of knowing where to find network resources—files and programs in various FTP repositories. Users can search by filename using wildcards and other options. ARCHIE is accessible via local clients, Telnet, or email.

WHOIS, X.500 and NETFIND help users find people and computers. WHOIS queries a central database for registered network users and hosts. X.500 is a more advanced directory service. NETFIND helps locate an email address or information about someone or a host, using multiple database lookups.
sections.eli5: When you want to find something on the Internet, different tools help with different jobs. WAIS searches documents, ARCHIE finds files, and WHOIS/X.500/NETFIND find people and computers.

sections.title: File Transfer Tools
sections.content:
TRICKLE and BITFTP are specialized servers for getting files easily and efficiently. Unlike standard FTP, which requires interactive use, these tools accept requests via email. TRICKLE can retrieve and mail back files in multiple parts if needed. BITFTP (File Transfer via Bitnet) serves users on BITNET, EARN and JANET networks who may not have full Internet connectivity but have email access.

These tools address the practical problem that not all users have direct FTP access, and for those who do, email-based requests offer convenience. Both are particularly valuable for networks with limited connectivity or bandwidth constraints.
sections.eli5: TRICKLE and BITFTP let you request files by email instead of using FTP directly. This is useful if you don't have full Internet access or want to request files offline.

sections.title: Discussion and Mailing List Tools
sections.content:
LISTSERV (version 1.7f) is a mailing list server that manages automated discussion groups. It accepts commands via email to subscribe, unsubscribe, list available groups, retrieve files and manage databases. LISTSERV can manage multiple mailing lists and supports file archives and database searching.

NETNEWS (USENET) is perhaps the most popular network resource. It is a system of discussion groups (newsgroups) organized in a hierarchy (like comp.infosystems.gopher) covering virtually every conceivable topic. Users read and post messages using newsreader software. Netnews differs from LISTSERV in that discussion happens in public forums rather than private email lists, and the infrastructure is distributed across many servers rather than centralized.
sections.eli5: LISTSERV and Netnews are two ways to have group discussions on the Internet. LISTSERV uses email; Netnews uses public discussion groups called newsgroups.

sections.title: Additional Tools
sections.content:
The RFC also describes six additional tools not mainstream enough for full coverage. ASTRA is a catalog of resources available on EARN/Bitnet. NETSERV and MAILBASE are mailing list systems used on European academic networks. PROSPERO is a distributed file system still in development. IRC (Internet Relay Chat) is for real-time typed conversations. RELAY is a mailing list tool.

Additionally, the RFC's appendix lists freely available client software for Gopher, World-Wide Web, WAIS, and Netnews newsreaders, covering platforms from Unix and X-Windows to Macintosh, MS-DOS, OS/2 and VMS. This comprehensive list helps users find appropriate tools for their systems.
sections.eli5: Beyond the main twelve tools, the guide mentions a few others that are more specialized or regional. It also lists where to find free software to use these tools on your computer.
